questions.title: Why does the importance ratio in GRPO fail to satisfy the principles of importance sampling?
questions.question_body: In the GRPO algorithm, the importance weight is defined per token as \(w_{i,t}(\theta) = \frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{i,t}\mid x, y_{i,<t})}{\pi_{\theta_{old}}(y_{i,t}\mid x, y_{i,<t})}\). The paper argues that this is a misapplication of importance sampling because it is based on a single sample from each next‑token distribution. Could someone walk through a concrete example showing why this single‑sample ratio does not correctly re‑weight expectations, and how the variance grows with sequence length?

questions.title: How is the sequence‑level importance ratio \(s_i(\theta)\) derived from token‑level ratios?
questions.question_body: GSPO defines \(s_i(\theta) = \left(\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_i\mid x)}{\pi_{\theta_{old}}(y_i\mid x)}\right)^{1/|y_i|} = \exp\left( \frac{1}{|y_i|}\sum_{t=1}^{|y_i|} \log \frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{i,t}\mid x, y_{i,<t})}{\pi_{\theta_{old}}(y_{i,t}\mid x, y_{i,<t})} \right)\). Why do the authors take the \(1/|y_i|\) power (or equivalently length‑normalize the log‑ratio)? What would happen if we omitted this normalization?

questions.title: What is the intuition behind using group‑based advantage normalization in GSPO?
questions.question_body: Both GRPO and GSPO compute \(\widehat{A}_i = \frac{r(x,y_i) - \mathrm{mean}(\{r(x,y_j)\})}{\mathrm{std}(\{r(x,y_j)\})}\). How does this ‘relative advantage’ differ from a vanilla advantage estimate using a value model, and why is it important for stability when the reward is defined at the sequence level?

questions.title: Why does clipping at the sequence level (GSPO) lead to a higher fraction of clipped tokens yet better training efficiency?
questions.question_body: Figure 2 in the paper shows that GSPO clips two orders of magnitude more tokens than GRPO, but still outperforms it. Is there an analytical explanation for why discarding many tokens can improve sample efficiency? How does sequence‑level clipping affect gradient variance compared to token‑level clipping?

questions.title: How does expert‑activation volatility in MoE models break GRPO’s token‑level importance ratios?
questions.question_body: The authors claim that after each gradient update, about 10% of experts activated for a given token change, causing large fluctuations in \(w_{i,t}(θ)\. Could someone clarify why this change in routing leads to invalid importance weights, and why GSPO’s sequence‑level ratio is robust to such routing changes?

questions.title: What exactly is the ‘Routing Replay’ strategy and why is it unnecessary for GSPO?
questions.question_body: In GRPO training of MoE models, Routing Replay caches the routing decisions of the old policy and forces the new policy to use the same experts when computing token‑level ratios. How is this implemented in practice (e.g., memory overhead, API changes), and why does GSPO avoid needing this mechanism altogether?

questions.title: When would one prefer GSPO-token over plain GSPO?
questions.question_body: GSPO-token introduces a per‑token advantage \(\widehat{A}_{i,t}\) while keeping the same objective value as GSPO when all token advantages are equal. In what scenarios (e.g., multi‑turn dialogue, fine‑grained credit assignment) does having token‑wise advantages provide a measurable benefit, and does it affect stability or compute cost?

questions.title: How does length normalization in the sequence importance ratio affect the clipping range selection?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions that without length normalization, "likelihood changes of a few tokens can result in dramatic fluctuations" and that clipping ranges differ by orders of magnitude between GSPO and GRPO. Could anyone elaborate on how to set appropriate clipping bounds for different response lengths, and whether adaptive clipping based on length is advisable?

questions.<title>: Is it theoretically valid to reuse inference‑engine likelihoods for RL updates as suggested by GSPO?
questions.<question_body>: `GSPO` claims that because it only needs sequence‑level likelihoods, one can directly use those returned by an inference engine (e.g., vLLM) without recomputing with the training engine. Does this introduce bias due to precision differences (fp16 vs bf16), and under what conditions is this approximation safe? Are there any empirical studies confirming negligible impact on gradient estimates?
